m: To deliberately refrain from doing or consuming something.
e: Latin abstinere, “to hold oneself back”: abs- (away) + tenere (to hold). Came through Old French abstenir.
t: Same as « s’abstenir » (and l’abstention in a vote). You hold yourself away from the thing.

m: To make something bad better; improve.
e: From French améliorer, from Latin ad- + melior (better). The 18th-century English form added Latin-looking -ate.
t: Ameliorate = améliorer, word for word. Melior = meilleur.

m: Lack of interest, enthusiasm or concern.
e: Greek apatheia: a- (without) + pathos (feeling, suffering). The Stoics prized it as freedom from passion.
t: A-pathos = no feeling, the opposite of sympathy. Same as « apathie ».

m: Practising strict self-denial; a person who does so.
e: Greek askētikos, from askētēs (monk, hermit), from askein (to exercise, train). First used of athletes in training, then of hermits training the soul.
t: Picture a desert hermit training like an athlete, but for the soul: no food, no comfort. « Une vie ascétique ».

m: Extremely greedy for wealth.
e: Latin avaritia (greed), from avarus (greedy), from avere (to crave).
t: Molière’s « L’Avare », Harpagon clutching his cash box. Avaricious = avare, and greedy for more.

m: Hostile and aggressive; eager to fight.
e: Latin belligerare, “to wage war”: bellum (war) + gerere (to carry on).
t: Bellum = war, as in « belliqueux ». A belligerent client is looking for a fight.

m: To find a way around an obstacle or rule.
e: Latin circumvenire, “to come around, surround”: circum (around) + venire (to come).
t: Circum + venir = to come around it. « Contourner la règle ».

m: To plan or bring about cleverly, often artificially.
e: Old French controver (to invent, find), from Late Latin contropare (to compare). A contrived plot feels artificial.
t: Old French controuver = to invent. A contrived ending is invented too obviously: « forcé, artificiel ».

m: To describe or outline precisely.
e: Latin delineare, “to sketch out”: de- + linea (line).
t: De + linea = drawing the lines of something. A good brief delineates the scope.

m: To indicate; to be the literal meaning of.
e: Latin denotare, “to mark out”: de- + notare (to mark), from nota (a mark).
t: Same as « dénoter ». Denote = the dictionary meaning; connote = the feeling around it.

m: Imitative of another’s work; unoriginal. (Also something derived.)
e: Late Latin derivativus, from derivare, “to draw off a stream”: de- + rivus (stream).
t: Water drawn off someone else’s stream. On the GRE, a derivative novel copies others.

m: To obtain or trace from a source.
e: Old French deriver, from Latin derivare: de- (from) + rivus (stream). Channelling water off a river.
t: Picture a channel drawing water from a river: you derive pleasure from a source.

m: Dissatisfied and no longer loyal, especially to authority.
e: dis- (reverse) + affect (to love, from Latin affectare). Literally having lost one’s affection.
t: Dis + affection: loyalty and love gone. Disaffected voters have given up on the party.

m: Drawing on a wide variety of sources or styles.
e: Greek eklektikos, “selective”, from eklegein: ek (out) + legein (to pick). Ancient philosophers who picked the best from every school.
t: Ek + legein = picking out the best bits. « Des goûts éclectiques ».

m: To make clear; explain.
e: Late Latin elucidare: e- (out) + lucidus (bright), from lux (light).
t: Same as « élucider ». Lux = light: you shine light on the mystery.

m: Famous and respected; outstanding.
e: Latin eminentem, from eminere, “to stand out”: e- + minere (to project). Related to Latin mons (mountain).
t: Une éminence = a hill that sticks out. An eminent scientist stands above the crowd. Not imminent (about to happen).

m: Lasting a very short time.
e: Greek ephēmeros, “lasting a day”: epi (on) + hēmera (day). The mayfly (éphémère) lives one day.
t: Same as « éphémère »: the mayfly that lives a single day. Ephemeral fame, ephemeral trends.

m: Based on a mistaken belief; misleading.
e: Latin fallaciosus, from fallacia (deceit), from fallere (to deceive). Same root as false and fail.
t: Identical to « fallacieux ». A fallacy is a trick of reasoning.

m: Pitifully sad and abandoned.
e: Old English forloren, past participle of forlēosan (to lose completely): for- + lēosan (to lose). Germanic, cousin of German verloren.
t: For-lorn = for-lost, verloren. A forlorn puppy left at the roadside.

m: To prevent a plan from succeeding; to annoy.
e: Latin frustrari (to disappoint, deceive), from frustra (in vain).
t: Frustra = in vain. On the GRE, “frustrate a plan” = déjouer: make it come to nothing.

m: Innocent and without deception.
e: guile (Old French guile, deceit, probably from Frankish, related to wile) + -less.
t: Guile = ruse. Guileless = sans ruse. A guileless child tells the truth without thinking.

m: Arrogantly superior and disdainful.
e: From haught, Old French haut (high), from Latin altus. The gh was added by analogy with high.
t: Haughty = hautain, from haut. Someone looking down on you from high up.

m: Someone who holds views contrary to accepted belief.
e: Greek hairetikos (able to choose), from hairesis (a choosing, a sect).
t: Hairesis = a choice. The heretic chose a different belief from the Church. Same as « hérétique ».

m: Unchanging; unable to be changed.
e: Latin immutabilis: in- (not) + mutare (to change), as in mutation.
t: No mutation possible. « Les lois immuables de la physique ».

m: Out of place; not in harmony with the surroundings.
e: Latin incongruus: in- (not) + congruus (agreeing), from congruere (to come together).
t: Same as « incongru ». Flip-flops at a board meeting.

m: Spreading gradually and harmfully, often unnoticed.
e: Latin insidiosus (cunning), from insidiae (ambush), from insidere (to sit in, lie in wait).
t: Insidiae = an ambush. An insidious disease lies in wait. Same as « insidieux ».

m: Travelling from place to place.
e: Late Latin itinerantem, from itinerari (to travel), from iter, itineris (journey).
t: Iter = journey, as in itinéraire. Itinerant workers follow the harvest.

m: Extreme, aggressive patriotism.
e: From a British music-hall song of 1878 supporting war against Russia, with the oath “by Jingo” (a euphemism for Jesus). Supporters were mocked as jingoes.
t: Picture Victorian Londoners singing for war in a music hall. Same idea as French « chauvinisme ».

m: Feeling or expressing great joy.
e: Latin iubilare (to shout with joy), originally a shepherd’s call; later linked to the Hebrew yobel (jubilee).
t: « Jubiler » = to rejoice. A jubilant crowd after a final whistle.

m: To place side by side for contrast.
e: French juxtaposer, from Latin iuxta (beside) + French poser (to place).
t: Identical to « juxtaposer ». A before/after slide juxtaposes two images.

m: Slow and relaxed; lacking energy.
e: Latin languidus (faint, weak), from languere (to be weak). Same root as languish.
t: Think « languir » and « langueur »: a languid afternoon in the heat.

m: Generous and forgiving, especially to a rival.
e: Latin magnanimus: magnus (great) + animus (soul, spirit).
t: Magna + anima = a great soul. Same as « magnanime ». The winner who praises the loser.

m: To calm someone’s anger or anxiety.
e: Latin mollificare: mollis (soft) + facere (to make).
t: Mollis = mou. To mollify an angry client = to soften them.

m: So small or unimportant it can be ignored.
e: From French négligeable, from Latin neglegere (to disregard): nec (not) + legere (to pick up).
t: Identical to « négligeable ». Something you can neglect.

m: Flamboyant confidence of style.
e: French panache, the plume of feathers on a helmet, from Italian pennacchio, from Latin penna (feather).
t: Cyrano de Bergerac’s last word: « mon panache »! The helmet plume worn with style.

m: Having developed abilities unusually early.
e: Latin praecox, “ripened early”: prae (before) + coquere (to cook, ripen).
t: Same as « précoce »: cooked before its time. A precocious child reads at three.

m: Ordinary, everyday.
e: Latin quotidianus, from quotidie (daily): quot (how many) + dies (day).
t: Quotidian = « quotidien ». Le Quotidien, your daily paper: totally ordinary.

m: Stubborn and unmanageable.
e: Latin refractarius (obstinate), from refringere (to break back): re- + frangere (to break).
t: Les « réfractaires » refused to submit (e.g. to the STO in WWII). Refractory = resists control.

m: Basic, elementary; undeveloped.
e: Latin rudimentum (first attempt), from rudis (rough, untrained).
t: Identical to « rudimentaire ». Rudis = raw, rough.

m: False; not genuine or valid.
e: Late Latin spurius (illegitimate, of unknown father).
t: Spurius = illegitimate child: a spurious argument doesn’t come from a real source.

m: Very loyal and committed.
e: Old French estanche (watertight), from estanchier (to stop a flow). Watertight → reliable → loyal.
t: Étanche = watertight! A staunch ally never leaks.

m: To include within a larger group.
e: Modern Latin subsumere: sub (under) + sumere (to take).
t: Take under: the smaller category is taken under the bigger one.

m: To replace, often by force or scheming.
e: Latin supplantare, “to trip up”: sub (under) + planta (sole of the foot).
t: Same as « supplanter »: you trip someone up and take their place.

m: Equivalent in seriousness to.
e: Anglo-French tant amunter, “to amount to as much”: tant (so much) + amonter (to go up, amount).
t: Tant + monter = amounts to as much. Silence is tantamount to consent.

m: Holding firmly; persistent.
e: Latin tenax, tenacis, from tenere (to hold).
t: Same as « tenace »: a grip that won’t let go.

m: A false, absurd or distorted version of something.
e: French travesti (disguised), from Italian travestire: tra- (across) + vestire (to dress).
t: « Travesti » = dressed up as something else. A travesty of justice is justice in disguise.

m: Guilty of betrayal; also hazardous.
e: Old French trecherous, from trechier (to cheat, trick).
t: Think « tricher »: a treacherous friend cheats you; a treacherous road tricks your tyres.

m: Leaving no doubt; unambiguous.
e: un- + equivocal, from Late Latin aequivocus: aequus (equal) + vox (voice).
t: Exactly « sans équivoque »: only one voice speaking.

m: Showing strong, forceful feeling.
e: Latin vehementem (impetuous, violent), possibly from vehere (to carry) + mens (mind): carried away.
t: Same as « véhément »: a mind carried away by passion.

m: To speak or write about in an abusive, disparaging way.
e: Late Latin vilificare: vilis (cheap, base) + facere (to make).
t: Make vile = « vilipender ». The tabloids vilified her.
